requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in fly-fishing activities and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. Name and explain five safety practices you should always follow while fly-fishing. (b) Discuss the prevention of and treatment for the following health concerns that could occur while fly-fishing: cuts and scratches, puncture wounds, insect bites, hypothermia, dehydration, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and sunburn. (c) Explain how to remove a hook that has lodged in someone's arm.

pamphlet_excerpts: Gentle Sport Fly-fishing: Even a gentle sport like fly-fishing can come with its perils.
Agood Angler Well-versed: Agood angler will be well-versed in first-aid for cuts, scratches, puncture wounds, and insect bites and stings.
Cuts Scratches Wounds: Cuts and scratches are wounds, openings in the skinand tissues that can allow germs to enter the body and causeinfection.
Wash Minor Scratches: Wash minor scratches and cuts with soap and water.
step_by_step_procedure: Camping Trips And rebandage: On camping trips, clean and rebandage small wounds daily.
Larger Cuts Treated: Larger cuts should be treated with direct pressure to stopbleeding, then cleaned as well as possible to limit infection.
Cover Open Wound: Cover an open wound with a sterile gauze pad or clean cloththat has been folded to make a pad.
Hold Pad Position with: Hold the pad in position with tape, a cravat bandage, or other binder.

pamphlet_excerpts: Lines Vary Weight: Lines vary by weight, and must be matched to the rod.
They Come Different: They come in different styles (called tapers) and colors and are designed either to float onthe surface of the water or to sink to different depths.
Intermediate Lines Example: Intermediate lines, for example, sink very slowly and canbe fished just below the surface.
Heavily Weighted Lines: Heavily weighted lines sinkquite rapidly and are designed to get down deep very quickly.
step_by_step_procedure: Fly-fishing Done Floating: Most fly-fishing is done with floating lines, which are the easiest to cast and control.
But There Times: But there are times and conditions whenfish lie deeply in the water and are not feeding at or near the surface.
Sinking Line Then: A sinking line is then useful to get the fly down to them.
Sinking Lines Usuallycome: Sinking lines usuallycome in drab, darker colors so that the fish cannot spot them.

requirements.req_text: Demonstrate how to tie proper knots to prepare a fly rod for fishing: (a) Tie backing to the arbor of a fly reel spool using an arbor knot. (b) Tie backing to the fly line using a nail (tube) knot. (c) Attach a leader to the fly line using a nail (tube) knot or a loop-to-loop connection. (d) Add a tippet to a leader using a surgeon's knot or a loop-to-loop connection. (e) Tie a fly onto the terminal end of the leader using an improved clinch knot.

pamphlet_excerpts: Assemble Gear Systematically: Assemble the gear systematically for trouble-free performance.
Previously Discussed: All of the previously discussed elements of a properlybalanced fly-fishing outfit must be assembled properly.
Beginby Attaching Reel: Beginby attaching the reel to the seat on the rod.
Thehandle Side Hand: Make sure thehandle is on the side of the hand you intend to reel.
step_by_step_procedure: Whenreeling Line Come: Whenreeling in the line, it should come into the bottom of the reel, and the drag should be engaged if the line is pulled out.
Theinner Workings Reel: Theinner workings of the reel may need to be adjusted to usethe handle on the preferred side.
Now Run Point: Now, run the point of thebacking through the stripping guide of the rod and attach thebacking to the reel spool using an arbor knot.
Attach Backing Reel: Attach the backing to the reel spool with an arbor knot.

step_by_step_procedure: Length Line Front: With that length of line in front of you, more or less in a straight line, start with the rod tip down near the ground orthe surface of the water.

step_by_step_procedure: Tarpon Largest Reach: Tarpon are the largest of the three and can reach weights of morethan 150 pounds.

Fishfor Few Hours: Whether you fishfor a few hours, an entire day, or plan to camp and fish, it isimportant to minimize your impact on the land.
High-useareas Concentrate: In high-useareas, concentrate your activity where vegetation is alreadyabsent.
step_by_step_procedure: Wading Gear Reduce: Use wading gear to reduce stream and lakeside impact.
Existing Trails Select: Use existing trails and select designated or existing fishingareas.
Remote Less-traveled Areas: In more remote, less-traveled areas, avoid creating newtrails that cause erosion, and avoid places where impacts arejust beginning to show.
Camping Overnight Camp: If camping overnight, always camp at least 200 feet fromshorelines.

pamphlet_excerpts: There Recipes Cooking: There are as many recipes for cooking a freshly caught fishas there are anglers.
Proper Cleaning Preparation: Proper cleaning and preparation of a fishbefore cooking will help ensure success with whatever cookingmethod you choose.
Follow Leave Trace: Follow the Leave No Trace Seven Principles and the Outdoor Code and local regulations for proper disposal of all fishentrails, skeletons, and other.
Areas Youshould Treat: In many areas, youshould treat this waste as you would human waste.
step_by_step_procedure: Cover Area Brown: Step 1, Cover the area with brown paper or newspaper.
Cut Downthe Backside: To skin the fish, cut downthe backside and loosenthe skin around the fins.
Remove Skin Withpliers: Remove the skin withpliers; pull the skin down from head to tail and cutit off at the tail.
Start Cut Run: Step 2, Start at the cut made in step 1 and run the point ofthe knife alongside the backbone, down to where it starts toclick along the tops of the ribs.
